---
title: "Getting started"
---

## Installation

```bash
composer require phpstats/phplyr
```

### Requirements

- PHP 8.3, 8.4, or 8.5. CI tests all three on Linux. Pipelines written with
  the pipe operator `|>` need PHP 8.5, and method chains run on all three.
- The mbstring extension, which phplyr requires.
- The PDO extension, which phibble requires.

Composer installs phibble (0.3, 0.4, or 0.5), which provides the tables, and
`symfony/polyfill-php84`, which provides PHP 8.4's functions on PHP 8.3.

### Optional features

**Statistical models.** `lm()`, `glm()`, `lmer()`, and `glmer()` call phit's
model functions. Either of two implementations provides them, and phplyr
calls both the same way:

- The [phit](https://github.com/phpstats/phit) extension, written in Rust.
  phplyr works with phit 0.1 and later. CI builds it from phit's main branch.
- [phit-polyfill](https://github.com/phpstats/phit-polyfill), the same
  functions in PHP, for systems where the extension cannot be installed. CI
  tests phplyr with phit-polyfill 0.3. Install it with
  `composer require phpstats/phit-polyfill`. [Models](reference/models.qmd)
  describes what it leaves out.

**Native descriptive statistics.** With the phit extension loaded, `mean()`,
`sd()`, `var_()`, `median()`, and `quantile()` call phit's statistics
functions. Without the extension, including with phit-polyfill, they run in
PHP and give the same results.

**Polars.** The [phpolars](https://github.com/phpstats/phpolars) extension
provides phibble's `PolarsTable`, which runs a pipeline in Polars. See
[Compatibility and limitations](compatibility.qmd#backends).

**Transliteration of names.** With the intl extension, `make_clean_names()`
and `clean_names()` transliterate non-ASCII names the way R's janitor does.
Without it, they use iconv, and some names can differ from janitor's. See
[janitor](reference/janitor.qmd).

**Database tables.** `Phibble\tbl()` runs a pipeline as SQL through PDO. It
needs the PDO driver for the database: SQLite, PostgreSQL, or MySQL. See
[Databases and expressions](reference/databases.qmd).

## A first script

Create a Composer project in an empty directory and download the example data,
test scores from 250 students in 12 schools:

```bash
composer require phpstats/phplyr
curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/phpstats/phplyr/v0.4.3/docs/data/schools.csv
```

Save one of the scripts below as `first.php` and run `php first.php`. Both
print the five schools with the highest average score among students who
studied at least five hours.

{{< include examples/_first-pipeline.md >}}

The other examples in this documentation leave out the `require` line and the
`use` imports, which the next section describes. Their CSV files are in the
repository's [docs/data](https://github.com/phpstats/phplyr/tree/main/docs/data)
directory, and the snippets on this page use `$schools` from the first
script.

## Imports

phplyr's functions are namespaced functions in `Phplyr`. Import the ones a file
uses with `use function`:

```php
use Phibble\DataFrame;
use function Phplyr\{phplyr, filter, mutate, group_by, summarize, arrange, desc, n, mean};
```

A method chain needs `phplyr()` and the helpers it calls, such as `n()`,
`mean()`, and `desc()`. The table functions are the chain's methods, so they
don't need importing.

Some phplyr functions have the same names as PHP built-in functions. In a file
that imports one of them, the bare name calls phplyr's function. Write a
leading backslash to call the built-in, as in `\count($array)`.

| phplyr functions | Where they are documented |
| --- | --- |
| `count`, `rename` | [Single-table functions](reference/single-table.qmd) |
| `min`, `max` | [Vector helpers](reference/vectors.qmd) |
| `abs`, `sqrt`, `exp`, `log`, `log10`, `round`, `floor` | [Expressions](reference/databases.qmd#expressions) |
| `str_replace`, `str_split`, `str_pad` | [Strings and dates](reference/strings-dates.qmd) |
| `extract`, `chop`, `pack`, `unpack` | [tidyr](reference/tidyr.qmd) |

A file that doesn't import these names is not affected.

## Loading data

phibble builds tables from CSV files, PDO queries, query builders, and PHP
arrays:

```php
$schools = DataFrame::fromCsv('schools.csv');
$rows = DataFrame::fromRows([['id' => 1, 'x' => 2.5], ['id' => 2, 'x' => null]]);
$cols = DataFrame::fromColumns(['id' => [1, 2], 'x' => [2.5, null]]);
```

`null` is a missing value, R's `NA`. A `DataFrame` is immutable, so every
function returns a new table and leaves its input unchanged. `echo $table`
prints the first rows in the format of R's tibble package.

## Pipelines

A table function such as `filter(...)` returns a closure that takes a table and
returns a new one. A pipeline applies such closures in order.

::: {.panel-tabset group="syntax"}

## PHP 8.5+

The pipe operator `|>` calls the closure on its right with the value on its
left:

```php
$out = $schools |>
    filter(fn ($r) => $r->score > 80) |>
    arrange(desc('score'));
```

## PHP 8.3–8.4

`phplyr($table)` starts a method chain. Each method calls the phplyr function
of the same name with the same arguments. A chained method is camelCase, so
`group_by()` is `->groupBy()` and `n_groups()` is `->nGroups()`. `get()`
returns the table:

```php
$out = phplyr($schools)
    ->filter(fn ($r) => $r->score > 80)
    ->arrange(desc('score'))
    ->get();
```

:::

The two forms give the same result, and the documentation shows both.

A method chain stays a chain while each method returns a table. These
functions return something else, and the chain returns that value:

| Functions | Return |
| --- | --- |
| `pull()`, `group_vars()`, `group_size()`, `group_indices()`, `group_rows()`, `group_split()`, `group_map()` | An array |
| `n_groups()` | An integer |
| `setequal()` | A boolean |
| `show_query()` | The SQL string |
| `lm()`, `glm()`, `lmer()`, `glmer()` | phit's result array |

`echo` prints a chain's table without `get()`. `->pipe($closure)` applies a
closure of your own and continues the chain with its result.

`pipe()` applies closures in order on every PHP version:

```php
$out = pipe($schools, filter(fn ($r) => $r->score > 80), arrange(desc('score')));
```

## Columns, row closures, and vector helpers

Columns are named with strings: `'score'` where dplyr takes a bare `score`.

A **row closure** is an ordinary PHP closure. It receives the row as a
`Phibble\Row`, whose columns read as `$r->score` or `$r['score']`, and the
table of the row's group as a second argument:

```php
mutate(gap: fn ($r) => $r->score - $r->prior_score)
filter(fn ($r, $group) => $r->score > mean('score')($group))
```

A **vector helper** is one of phplyr's functions for whole columns, such as
`lag('x')`, `cumsum('x')`, `min_rank('x')`, or `mean('x')`. It is evaluated
once per group. A summary helper in `mutate()` gives one value per group, and
that value is repeated on every row of the group:

{{< include examples/_grouping.md >}}

The first argument of a vector helper is the column. It can be a column name,
`col('x')`, another helper, or a row closure. Later arguments are values, so a
string there is a literal. Wrap a string in `col()` to refer to a column.

A third form, `col('x')->mul(2)`, builds an expression. Expressions give the
same results as the helpers in memory, and they let a pipeline run as SQL on a
database table. See [Databases and expressions](reference/databases.qmd).

## Named arguments and options

Functions that create columns name them with PHP named arguments:
`mutate(total: ...)`, `summarize(n: n())`. An option that dplyr writes with a
leading dot, such as `.by`, is written with a leading underscore, such as
`_by:`. Any other named argument is a column, so `mutate(_before: 'id')` places
the new columns and `mutate(before: 1)` makes a column called `before`.
[Underscored arguments](coming-from-dplyr.qmd#underscored-arguments) lists
them.

PHP does not allow positional arguments after named ones. Put `across()` and
other positional arguments first: `summarize(across(...), n: n())`.

## Printing and inspecting

`echo` prints a table. `glimpse()` prints one line per column and returns the
table unchanged, so it can sit inside a pipeline. `pull('x')` returns a column
as a PHP array, and `$table->toRows()` returns every row as an array.
